name: Sara Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Sara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and also what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a crew up in the mountain district, where the big job these days is fire-hardening the lines. After the fires three summers ago, the company's replacing old wooden poles with steel ones, putting covered wire through the forests and burying some lines near the towns. My morning starts with an AI tool that pulls together the weather, the wind and the fire-risk map, and I plan the day's work around it. I love the mountains and the feeling that we're stopping the next fire. What wears me out is the steep ground, you can spend half a day just getting a truck to the right spot.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What happens on a high fire-risk day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We don't do anything that could throw a spark, so no cutting or grinding near dry brush. Some days we switch to paperwork or training back at the yard, which my crew hates. My parents run the hardware store in town and my dad still asks me every Sunday after church whether the lines are safe yet, like I personally hold every pole up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Huh. I'd be a little disappointed, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame, because the tools I use are really good for planning. At the yard I'd say at least the fire maps were worth it. Online I don't post much, maybe I'd share something about it in my trades group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the job stays the same, which is fine. The fire work will keep us busy for years. I'd keep planning my days with a weather map and a coffee, which honestly isn't a bad life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going like now. Keep saving, I've got about a year put away and I keep adding to it. I'd keep using the AI tools and probably think more seriously about starting my own small contracting crew in a few years, since the fire work isn't going anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned starting your own crew. How serious is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty serious. There's more fire-hardening work than the company can do itself, and they hire contractors at good rates. I'd want my own trucks, my own crew, my own name on the door, like my parents have with the store.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's holding you back from doing it now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly experience on the business side. I know how to build a line, I'm still learning how to price a job and run payroll. My dad's been teaching me on the weekends, he's done the store's books for thirty years.

S0.say: She'd call it a shame since her planning tools are genuinely good, and say at the yard that at least the fire maps were worth it. She might share something in her trades group.
S0.think: The job stays the same, which is fine, since fire work will keep her busy for years. Planning days with a weather map and coffee isn't a bad life.
S0.do: Keeps working and saving, with about a year already put away. Keeps using AI tools and thinks more seriously about starting her own contracting crew, learning the business side from her father.
S0.quote: I'd keep planning my days with a weather map and a coffee, which honestly isn't a bad life.
S0.fieldNote: Sara is strongly entrepreneurial, already planning her own crew and learning bookkeeping from her father. She uses AI daily for fire and weather planning. Her family's hardware store is her model for independence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one that makes the most sense to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a good time to be someone who can learn. At the yard I'd tell my crew to get on the new kit early. With friends I'd say the people who adapt will be fine, and the ones waiting for someone to rescue them will struggle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this is my moment. If robots and AI make line work faster, a small crew can do what a big one used to. If one robot can do the work of two climbers, a small contractor like I want to be can suddenly bid on jobs the big firms used to own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the business sooner, maybe in two years instead of five. I'd use part of my savings to lease or buy whatever new kit actually works, like a robotic arm for live-line work or a drone for stringing. I'd keep my job while I built up the business on weekends at first. I'd learn every new tool going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited. A bit nervous about the money, but excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older guys on my crew who don't like change. Like Walt, he's been climbing these mountains for thirty years. I'd want to hire him, honestly, he knows things no robot does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people waiting to be rescued will struggle. Is that fair to people like Walt?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair question. Walt isn't waiting to be rescued, he's just good at what he does. I'd say it's on companies and small firms like mine to find a place for people like him, not on the government.

S1.say: She'd call it a good time to be someone who can learn, urging her crew onto the new kit early. With friends she'd say adapters will be fine while those waiting for rescue will struggle.
S1.think: This is her moment: robots and AI would let a small crew bid on jobs big firms used to own. She sees a chance to start her contracting business sooner.
S1.do: Starts her business in about two years instead of five, using savings to lease or buy proven kit like a live-line robotic arm or stringing drone. Keeps her job while building the business on weekends and learns every new tool.
S1.feel: Excited, with some nerves about the money.
S1.quote: If one robot can do the work of two climbers, a small contractor like I want to be can suddenly bid on jobs the big firms used to own.
S1.fieldNote: Sara sees opportunity rather than threat and plans to use automation to compete as a small contractor. When I gently challenged her line about people waiting to be rescued, she softened it for her older colleague Walt. Her answer was that companies, not government, should make room for such workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's very fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's huge and people need to move quickly. At the yard I'd tell everyone to get their savings in order and think about what they're good at beyond the tools. I'd post in my trades group about what I was doing, so others could copy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit worried, mostly about timing. If robots can do almost everything, the question becomes who owns them. I'd rather be the person who owns the robot than the person it replaced, and two years is barely enough to get the paperwork done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start my contracting business within the year, and use most of my savings to buy or lease robots and AI kit. I'd leave the company once I had my first contract. I'd hire a couple of people from my old crew to run and check the machines. I'd keep a few months of living costs aside, no matter what, because I know it could all fall over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. More excited than scared, but there's a lot that could go wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big firms could buy up all the robots first, and a small contractor like me gets squeezed out. Or the power company decides it doesn't need contractors at all. I'd be betting most of my savings on getting there first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years take away, compared with more time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to learn the business side properly. I'd be learning payroll and robot leasing at the same time. With more time, I'd get the basics sorted first.

S2.say: She'd call it huge and urge people to move fast, telling her yard to get savings in order and think about strengths beyond tools. She'd post in her trades group so others could copy her.
S2.think: She'd be a bit worried, mainly about timing, since the key question becomes who owns the robots. Two years is barely enough to get the paperwork done.
S2.do: Starts her contracting business within the year, putting most of her savings into robots and AI kit, and leaves the company once she lands a first contract. Hires former crewmates to run the machines while keeping a few months of living costs aside.
S2.feel: Uneasy, more excited than scared but aware of what could go wrong.
S2.quote: I'd rather be the person who owns the robot than the person it replaced, and two years is barely enough to get the paperwork done.
S2.fieldNote: Sara would bet most of her savings on owning robots rather than being replaced by them. Her main fear is big firms buying all the robots first and squeezing out small contractors. She keeps a small reserve aside, showing she understands the risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for people who start now. At the yard I'd keep telling the crew to think about where they'll be. With friends I'd say don't wait for someone else to fix this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years is about perfect for me. Five years is long enough to get my name on the door before the robots get theirs on the paycheque. I'd be thirty-two, with the business running and the robots working for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the business on the side in the first year, small contracts on weekends, so I learn the money side without risking everything. I'd keep my job for two or three years and keep saving. Then I'd buy or lease the robots and go full time. By the time it arrives, I'd want my own crew of people and machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It feels like a plan I can actually do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you bring with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Walt, if he'd come. And Josie, she's two years into her apprenticeship and sharp as anything. I'd want people who know the mountains, robots or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years buy you, compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A safer start. With two years I'd be betting everything at once. With five I can build up slowly and not lose my savings if the first year goes wrong.

S3.say: She'd say five years is enough for those who start now, urging her crew to think ahead and telling friends not to wait for someone else to fix things.
S3.think: Five years is about perfect for her to get her business established before robots take over payrolls. At 32 she'd have her business running with robots working for her.
S3.do: Starts the business on the side in the first year with small weekend contracts, keeping her job and saving for two or three years. Then buys or leases robots and goes full time with her own crew of people and machines.
S3.feel: Mostly calm, with a plan she can actually do.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough to get my name on the door before the robots get theirs on the paycheque.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Sara build up gradually and protect her savings, which suits her better than the two-year gamble. She'd bring along her older colleague Walt and a sharp apprentice, Josie. Her focus on people who know the mountains shows loyalty alongside her business drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty for anyone willing to work at it. At the yard I'd tell the young ones this is their chance to build something. With friends I'd say there's time to get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine, more than fine. I'd be thirty-seven, with years in the trade and years running my own crew. With ten years I could build the business the old way first, with people, and only bring in robots when they're proven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the business in a couple of years, with trucks and people, the normal way. I'd keep saving and learning the AI tools. In the later years, I'd bring in robots when they're cheap and reliable. I'd keep Walt and Josie on as long as I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Really calm, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that bothers you about this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents' store, maybe. If robots do everything, who needs a hardware store in a mountain town? I'd want to help them work out what's next, even if it's just retiring with something saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra five years change for you, compared with five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I don't have to rush. With five years, I'd be planning around the robots from day one. With ten, I can build a real business first and add them later.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is plenty for anyone willing to work, telling young workers it's their chance to build something and friends there's time to prepare.
S4.think: She'd be more than fine at 37, with years in the trade and running her own crew. She could build the business the traditional way first and add robots once proven.
S4.do: Starts the business in a couple of years with trucks and people, keeps saving and learning AI tools, and brings in robots later when cheap and reliable. Keeps her trusted crew members on as long as she can.
S4.quote: With ten years I could build the business the old way first, with people, and only bring in robots when they're proven.
S4.fieldNote: Sara is very relaxed with a decade, and her main concern shifts to her parents' hardware store. She'd build the business with people first and add robots only when proven. She treats the extra time as room to do things properly rather than rush.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd be betting everything at once, and so would everyone else. I'm not afraid of robots, I'm afraid of only having two years to buy one before somebody bigger does. What would help is making it easier for small businesses to get loans and lease the new kit, so it isn't only the big firms who own it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to small towns like mine. The store, the church, the school all depend on people having work here. If the big companies own all the robots, the money leaves town, and I'd hate that more than anything.

headlineQuote: I'm not afraid of robots, I'm afraid of only having two years to buy one before somebody bigger does.
portrait: Sara Ziegler is a 27-year-old crew lead fire-hardening power lines in a mountain district, planning each day with an AI tool that pulls together weather, wind and fire-risk maps. She has about a year saved, is close to her parents who run the town hardware store, and is already learning the business side so she can start her own contracting crew. She is calm in the plateau and excited by steady disruption, uneasy only about the timing in the two-year picture, and calm again with five or ten years. Her answer to every picture is to own the robots rather than be replaced by them, while keeping her loyal crew and protecting her town.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she'd have to bet everything at once and might lose out to bigger firms buying the robots first.
whatWouldHelp: Making it easier for small businesses to get loans and lease the new kit, so the big firms aren't the only ones who own it.
